newsitem.title: MADAGASCAR: Madagascar former ruler tipped to win presidency.
newsitem.headline: Madagascar former ruler tipped to win presidency.

text.p: Madagascar goes to the polls on Sunday with former Marxist military ruler Didier Ratsiraka tipped to defeat his rival for the presidency.
Ratsiraka, 60, and former president Albert Zafy, 69 whose impeachment by parliament in September forced the two-round election, faced off in a lacklustre televised debate on Friday.

Zafy focused on the 16 years under Ratsiraka which ended with the last presidential election in 1993, following nationwide strikes and protests that forced him to give in to democracy after heavy repression.
He concentrated on Ratsiraka's Revolutionary Socialist rule and especially on killings in August 1991 when troops on his orders fired on protesters heading for the presidential palace.

Ratsiraka, a retired admiral, explained his programme to set up a "humanistic and ecological republic" in Madagascar, the world's fourth largest island of 14 million people who live in chronic poverty with inflation running at 50 percent per year.

Zafy, a former surgeon known for his trademark straw hat, showed during the debate he did not know the rate of inflation in Madagascar and he confused the code for investments and the code for "free industrial zones" as well as other facts.
Zafy attempted to portray himself as a known populist while Ratsiraka demonstrated his grasp of technicalities, prompting one Antananrivo newspaper on Sunday to describe him as a pedant.
Nevertheless Ratsiraka, widely known as "the red admiral" for his self-styled Marxism based on his own "Little Red Book", remains popular among the very poor on the island.

Ratsiraka, who became a reluctant free market supporter in the early 1990s, is tipped to take 60 percent of the vote in the second round of the presidential election. Some six million people are eligible to vote but a low-turnout is expected after more than 40 percent voted in the first round on November 3.
Ratsiraka and Zafy gained 36.61 percent and 23.39 percent respectively in the first round when none of the 15 candidates was able to secure the 50 percent of the vote to win outright.
Following Friday's debate, interim president Norbert Ratsirahonana, prime minister before the election, said he was willing to be his prime minister again as Zafy has promised.
Ratsirahonana, who took 10 percent of the vote in November, said he wanted to continue his campaign to win new loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank suspended in 1992.
The IMF has set aside nearly $50 million for new loans.

Ratsiraka returned from 19 months of voluntary exile in France at the end of September for the campaign and the high level of support for him surprised many observers though Zafy's rule was marked by a series of political and economic crises.
Political squabbling under Zafy since 1993 in the former French colony has frustrated plans to improve life for the islanders, who remain among the poorest people in the world.
